tools.name: Barina GPU Collatz Verifier
tools.approach: GPU-accelerated sieve with modular arithmetic shortcuts. Uses 2^32 lookup table for sieve acceleration. Distributed across supercomputers.
tools.performance: Verified up to 2^71. Total acceleration 1335x over naive CPU. Processes ~1.31 × 10^12 numbers/sec on GPU.
tools.limitations: Requires NVIDIA GPU. Focused on convergence verification, not delay record search.

tools.name: Roosendaal Distributed Project
tools.approach: Distributed computing project for class records, delay records, path records. Uses NVIDIA GPU workers.
tools.performance: 35,900 blocks completed (each 10^12 numbers). Takes 5-10 days per block of 10,000 units on NVIDIA GPU.
tools.limitations: Closed-source distributed client. Not available for independent use.

tools.name: rogerdahl/cuda-collatz
tools.approach: CUDA-based delay record calculator. Claims to be 'world's fastest Collatz Delay Record calculator'.
tools.performance: Focused specifically on delay records. Uses GPU parallelism.

tools.name: Honda et al. GPU Verifier
tools.approach: GPU exhaustive verification. GeForce GTX TITAN X. Batch processing of 64-bit numbers.
tools.performance: 1.31 × 10^12 64-bit numbers/sec on GPU. 249x speedup over CPU.
tools.limitations: 2017 era hardware. Not optimized for delay search.

tools.name: yoyo@home Collatz Project
tools.approach: BOINC distributed computing. Checked all numbers up to 87 × 2^60 for convergence.
tools.performance: Found 4 new path records during 2017 search. Crowdsourced computation.
tools.limitations: BOINC infrastructure required. No longer actively running Collatz tasks.

tools.name: Wei Ren extremely large integer verifier
tools.approach: Bit-level computation for extremely large numbers (up to 2^100000 - 1). Converts numerical computation to bit operations.
tools.performance: Verified 2^100000 - 1 reaches 1. Uses hard disk for intermediate values.
tools.limitations: Single-number verification, not range scanning. Very slow for systematic search.

performance_gap_targeted: No existing tool specifically targets OEIS A284668 computation. The gap is: efficiently finding the number with maximum stopping time within a decade [10^(n-1), 10^n). This requires a hybrid approach: sieve to eliminate low-delay candidates, then full computation on survivors. Our approach will use Python with gmpy2 for arbitrary precision, multiprocessing for 20-core parallelism, and a k-step shortcut engine to achieve competitive speed without GPU.
